Is 35 too late to move into tech?

We hear that question in almost every intake.

The switchers who do well here aren't the ones who memorised the most syntax before applying. They're the ones who already know how to handle a difficult stakeholder, run a process, own a mistake and finish what they started. None of that expires at 35.

What we add is the technical layer: structured training, a mentor, and real enterprise project work — while you're employed and paid from Day 1.

If you've been telling yourself you left it too late, treat that as a hypothesis, not a fact. Then test it.

decisions.pattern: Draft OPENS WITH A QUESTION
decisions.draft:
Want to know what week 3 of training actually looks like?

08:45 — coffee, then standup. Yesterday, today, blockers. Trainees run it, mentors listen.
09:15 — paired work on the sprint ticket. One drives, one reviews, then they swap.
11:00 — a code review that turns into a long conversation about naming and null checks. Worth it.
13:00 — mentor session: why the layer you're building exists in an enterprise system at all.
15:00 — back to the ticket, now with a clearer idea of what 'done' means.
16:30 — write down what broke and why, so tomorrow starts faster.

Week 3 is where the syntax stops feeling like flashcards and starts feeling like a job. Because it is one.

#DayInTheLife #UpskillToday #GECOAsia #TechTraining #LearnToCode

Curious what's inside our Java full-stack track?

Backend: Java fundamentals, OOP and collections, then Spring Boot — REST APIs, persistence, transaction handling, testing.
Frontend: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, then a component framework, so you can build the screen that consumes the API you just wrote.
Around it: Git and branching, code review, CI basics, debugging, reading logs, and writing tickets someone else can pick up.

The point isn't a certificate at the end. It's being useful on an enterprise project — where the code has history, the requirements change, and someone has to maintain what you wrote.

Trainees on this track are employed from Day 1 and work with a mentor throughout.

"Am I too late?" It's the question we hear most from people considering a switch into tech at 35, 40 or 45.

Here's the honest answer: your age isn't the obstacle. Unclear expectations are.

Enterprise teams need people who can handle a stakeholder who changes their mind, write a clear email, and stay calm during an incident. If you've spent a decade in operations, retail or finance, you already have that. What you need is the technical layer on top — and that's the part we train.

At Upskill Today you're hired from Day 1, so the journey isn't a gamble you fund alone. You learn, you get reviewed, you work on real project tasks.

Switching careers doesn't have to be a game-changing leap of faith. It can be a series of small, well-supported steps that unlock a role you can actually hold down.

That's the game-changing advice our trainees repeat back months later — and the kind of guidance you only unlock from someone who has done the work.

decisions.pattern: Draft uses hype words (revolutionary, game-changing, unlock, journey)
decisions.draft:
What week 3 actually looks like at Upskill Today. No revolutionary format, just a routine that works.

09:00 — Stand-up. Yesterday's blockers, today's plan. Two minutes each, same as a client team.
09:30 — Guided lab. This week: reading an existing codebase instead of writing a fresh one.
12:30 — Lunch, usually with the same argument about naming conventions.
13:30 — Project task on a simulated enterprise brief. Requirements are incomplete on purpose.
16:00 — Code review with a mentor. Direct, specific, sometimes uncomfortable.
17:00 — Notes on what to fix tomorrow.

Week 3 is where the journey stops feeling like a course. People start unlocking the habit that matters most on real projects: asking what the requirement actually means before building anything.

Small shift. Game-changing on a delivery team.

"So is this a bootcamp or a job?"

We get this question every week, so let's be plain about it.

When you join Upskill Today, you're hired. From Day 1. You're on payroll while you train, not paying tuition and hoping something lands at the end.

The training is real, though. Structured tracks, mentors who have shipped enterprise systems, code reviews that don't let things slide. Then you move onto live projects with GECO Asia's client teams — the kind with legacy systems, compliance requirements and stakeholders who change their minds.

That's the part most programmes can't simulate. You learn what "done" means when someone else has to run what you built.

We hire mid-career switchers and fresh graduates. What we look for isn't a CS pedigree. It's evidence you can learn something hard and keep going when it stops being fun.

Employed first. Trained properly. Deployed on work that matters.

The hardest part of enterprise AI isn't the model. It's the spreadsheet with four versions of the same customer name.

Our data and AI track starts there, on purpose.

You'll spend real time on SQL and Python, on cleaning and joining data that was never designed to be joined, and on building pipelines someone else can rerun without you. Then dashboards and reporting that a business head will actually read. Then the modelling layer — classical ML fundamentals, evaluation, and where generative AI tooling genuinely helps versus where it quietly makes things up.

We also cover the unglamorous side: access controls, PII, audit trails, documenting how a number was produced. In a regulated client environment, that's the difference between a pilot and something that goes live.

You join as an employee from Day 1 and train toward a live GECO Asia client project. Graduates and mid-career switchers both come through this track — analysts, engineers, people from finance ops who are tired of doing the same reconciliation by hand every month.

If you like being the person who finds out what's actually true, this is that job.

Every few months the same conversation resurfaces in a leadership meeting, and it always sounds slightly different but it is always the same conversation.

'We can't find the people we need.'

I have heard it from CTOs, from delivery heads, from programme managers who are three weeks from a go-live and staring at a resource plan that does not add up. And every time, the options presented are the same two options.

Option one: pay a premium for scarce senior contractors and hope they are still available next quarter. Option two: leave the requisition open, wait, and quietly move the deadline.

Both are reactive. Both treat talent as something you buy at the moment of maximum pain, which is the most expensive moment to buy anything.

There is a third option, and it is not glamorous, and it does not show results this sprint. You build a local pipeline before you need it.

What do I mean by local? I mean people who are already here. The operations analyst who understands your claims rules better than any new graduate you could import. The logistics coordinator who knows exactly where the process breaks. The career returner. The graduate from a university you have never recruited from.

Mid-career switchers in particular carry something that is genuinely hard to teach: domain context. A former claims analyst does not need three weeks of workshops to understand why the business rules are the way they are. They already lived it. What they need is the technical layer, and that is a trainable gap.

This is the model we run at Upskill Today, a GECO Asia division. Hire from Day 1, train on the systems our partners actually operate, then deploy onto live enterprise projects.

It is slower than buying a contractor. It is also how you stop having this same conversation every quarter.

Build the bench before you need the bench.

Curious how others are thinking about this — are you building ahead of demand, or hiring into it?

#TalentPipeline #LocalTalent #TechTalent #UpskillToday #GECOAsia #WorkforceDevelopment #EnterpriseDelivery
